# Data provenance and credit

Every source below is registered in
[`src/migratlas/catalog/registry.yaml`](../../src/migratlas/catalog/registry.yaml) with
its licence, citation and sensitivity classification. Nothing may be ingested that is
not described there.

None of this data is ours. Cloning this repository gives you the code, not the data —
each source carries its own terms.

## Dark Ecology Dataset — daily time series of aerial biomass, 1995–2025

- **id** `darkecology_daily`
- **evidence type** `flux` · **realm** `aerial` · **taxon scope** `unattributed`
- **landing page** https://darkecology.github.io/dataset/
- **DOI** [10.5281/zenodo.18433334](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18433334)
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - CC BY permits redistribution of derived products with attribution.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default

**Cite as**

> Dark Ecology project (2026). Dark Ecology Dataset: Measurements of Biological Activity in US Weather Radar — Time Series Data from 1995–2025, v1.1.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18433334

**Caveats**

Measures aerial biomass, not birds: MistNet separates precipitation from biology, not birds from bats from insects. `traffic` is vertically and temporally integrated, so it carries no height information — use the profiles product for flight altitude. Station histories are uneven across 1995–2025 and the NEXRAD dual-polarisation upgrade around 2011–2013 is a step change in the instrument that must be modelled as a break rather than read as a biological trend; the daily product does not label hardware generation, so upgrade dates have to come from elsewhere. Nights with a high `fraction_missing` must be excluded before computing passage quantiles.

## Dark Ecology Dataset — vertical profiles of aerial biomass, 1995–2025

- **id** `darkecology_profiles`
- **evidence type** `flux` · **realm** `aerial` · **taxon scope** `unattributed`
- **landing page** https://darkecology.github.io/dataset/
- **DOI** [10.5281/zenodo.13345173](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13345173)
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - CC BY permits redistribution of derived products with attribution.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default

**Cite as**

> Dark Ecology project (2026). Dark Ecology Dataset: Measurements of Biological Activity in US Weather Radar — Vertical Profiles, v1.1.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13345173

**Caveats**

Not yet ingested. Roughly 220 GiB across seven Zenodo records in five-year blocks, one CSV per radar volume scan under profiles/YYYY/MM/DD/STATION/. Height-resolved, so it is the source for flight-altitude questions — but for seasonal passage timing the daily product answers the same question from 159 MiB, so this stays unfetched until altitude is actually the question.

## MegaMove — global space use of marine megafauna

- **id** `megamove`
- **evidence type** `abundance_surface` · **realm** `marine` · **taxon scope** `exact`
- **landing page** https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.x95x69ptv
- **DOI** [10.5061/dryad.x95x69ptv](https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.x95x69ptv)
- **licence** [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - CC0 waives rights, but citation is an academic obligation regardless and the authors asked for it. One component (anthropogenic threats) is hosted separately under different terms and is not ingested.
- **sensitivity** `low` by default

**Cite as**

> Sequeira, A. M. M. et al. (2025) Global tracking of marine megafauna space use reveals how to achieve conservation targets. Science. Data: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.x95x69ptv

**Caveats**

Derived products only — 1-degree gridded space use, not raw tracks. Grid cell counts of tracked individuals reflect research effort as much as animal distribution; the published bias-testing datasets must be used alongside them. Covers 1985–2018, so it does not speak to the last several years.

## OBIS speciesgrids — gridded marine species distributions (H3 level 7)

- **id** `obis_speciesgrids`
- **evidence type** `abundance_surface` · **realm** `marine` · **taxon scope** `exact`
- **landing page** https://github.com/iobis/speciesgrids
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - Derived from OBIS and GBIF occurrence snapshots, whose contributing datasets carry their own terms; cite OBIS and GBIF as well as this product.
- **sensitivity** `low` by default

**Cite as**

> OBIS (2026). speciesgrids: WoRMS-aligned gridded marine species distributions derived from OBIS and GBIF occurrence snapshots. Ocean Biodiversity Information System. https://github.com/iobis/speciesgrids

**Caveats**

Occurrence records per H3 cell, not individuals and not abundance — this measures sampling effort as much as distribution, and must never be summed against a relative-abundance or tracked-individual surface. Not a movement product: there is no within-year timing, only a min/max year per cell. Ingest is deliberately bounded to vertebrate and cephalopod classes; the full product is 257k species and 43M cells dominated by gastropods, crustaceans and diatoms, and Teleostei is excluded for now because it adds 27k species each needing a Backbone lookup. Upstream keys species by WoRMS AphiaID, so names are resolved through the GBIF Backbone and any species that fails to resolve is dropped and logged rather than published without a key. Finally, "marine" here is generous: because OBIS aggregates coastal and estuarine records from GBIF, the vertebrate slice includes plainly non-marine birds — mallard, killdeer and great blue heron are among the widest-ranging species by cell count. Any genuinely marine analysis needs a further filter on top of this ingest.

## eBird Status and Trends — weekly relative abundance (2023 release)

- **id** `ebird_status_trends`
- **evidence type** `abundance_surface` · **realm** `aerial` · **taxon scope** `exact`
- **landing page** https://science.ebird.org/en/status-and-trends
- **licence** [eBird Status and Trends Products Terms of Use](https://ebird.org/about/products-access-terms-of-use)
- **redistribution** **not permitted**, attribution required, non-commercial only
  - Analysis and reported statistics only. Non-peer-reviewed use is capped at 50 species, which is why the species list is a fixed, curated constant rather than a query. Any published visualisation would additionally have to be shown exactly as downloaded, with the Cornell logo and citation embedded — a further reason nothing from here reaches the globe.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default

**Cite as**

> Fink, D., T. Auer, A. Johnston, M. Strimas-Mackey, S. Ligocki, O. Robinson, W. Hochachka, L. Jaromczyk, C. Crowley, K. Dunham, A. Stillman, I. Davies, A. Rodewald, V. Ruiz-Gutierrez, C. Wood (2023). eBird Status and Trends, Data Version: 2023. Cornell Lab of Ornithology, Ithaca, New York.

**Caveats**

A single modelled year at weekly resolution, not an annual time series — the 2023 release describes one representative year, so it can validate the SHAPE of a seasonal cycle but cannot corroborate a trend across years, and cannot speak to the 2012 instrument step. Relative abundance is standing stock, not passage flux: a station-level comparison against radar traffic must compare timing landmarks or rates of change, never levels. Release versions are not comparable to each other; the models change between them.

## FISHGLOB — 29 harmonised scientific bottom-trawl surveys

- **id** `fishglob`
- **evidence type** `survey_index` · **realm** `marine` · **taxon scope** `exact`
- **landing page** https://github.com/AquaAuma/FishGlob_data
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - CC BY 4.0 on the compilation. The contributing national surveys carry their own terms and their own citations; the data descriptor's Table 1 lists them and must be credited alongside FISHGLOB for any survey whose data is shown.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default

**Cite as**

> Maureaud, A. A., Palacios-Abrantes, J., Kitchel, Z., Mannocci, L., Pinsky, M. L., Fredston, A., Beukhof, E., Forrest, D. L., Frelat, R., Palomares, M. L. D., Pecuchet, L., Thorson, J. T., van Denderen, P. D., Merigot, B. (2024). FISHGLOB_data: an integrated dataset of fish biodiversity sampled with scientific bottom-trawl surveys. Scientific Data 11, 24. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41597-023-02866-w

**Caveats**

Continental-shelf trawlable ground only — North Atlantic, North Pacific and a few other shelves. No open ocean, no pelagic megafauna, almost nothing in the southern hemisphere, and nothing where a trawl cannot go. Survey footprints change across decades as stations are added and dropped, so any distribution metric must be restricted to consistently sampled cells or it measures where the ship went. Gear changes within several series and is a step change in the instrument, like the NEXRAD dual-polarisation upgrade. Catch in numbers is the standard basis for distribution centroids, but a trawl selects by size and behaviour and is not a census.

## NCEP North American Regional Reanalysis — pressure-level winds, 1979–present

- **id** `narr`
- **drivers only**, no evidence rows · **realm** `aerial`
- **landing page** https://psl.noaa.gov/data/gridded/data.narr.html
- **licence** [US Government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. §105)](https://www.noaa.gov/information-technology/open-data-dissemination)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - Public domain, so redistribution of derived products is unrestricted. Credit NOAA PSL as the distributor and cite Mesinger et al. 2006 as the reanalysis.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default

**Cite as**

> Mesinger, F., DiMego, G., Kalnay, E., Mitchell, K., Shafran, P. C., Ebisuzaki, W., Jović, D., Woollen, J., Rogers, E., Berbery, E. H., Ek, M. B., Fan, Y., Grumbine, R., Higgins, W., Li, H., Lin, Y., Manikin, G., Parrish, D., Shi, W. (2006). North American Regional Reanalysis. Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 87, 343–360. https://doi.org/10.1175/BAMS-87-3-343

**Caveats**

North America only — the Lambert Conformal domain stops at the continent, so this cannot serve a European or southern-hemisphere network and ERA5 via the Copernicus CDS is the substitute there (docs/adr/0006). A reanalysis is a model constrained by observations, not a measurement: its assimilated observing system changed across 1979–present, so a trend in a NARR variable is not automatically a trend in the atmosphere, and any trend computed from a quantity derived against it must be reported alongside the trend in the NARR term itself. 32 km cells mean a station near a coast or a mountain front is represented worse than an inland one; the ingest records each station's distance to its cell centre for that reason. Night winds here are means over the 00/03/06/09 UTC steps, which approximate but do not reproduce any individual station's true night boundaries.

## ERA5 monthly averaged reanalysis on single levels, 1940–present

- **id** `era5`
- **drivers only**, no evidence rows · **realm** `aerial`
- **landing page** https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/datasets/reanalysis-era5-single-levels-monthly-means
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - CC BY 4.0 permits redistribution of derived products with attribution. Copernicus asks that products be credited to the Copernicus Climate Change Service and that neither the European Commission nor ECMWF be represented as endorsing the result.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default
- **credential** `MIGRATLAS_CRED_CDS_TOKEN` required

**Cite as**

> Hersbach, H., Bell, B., Berrisford, P., Biavati, G., Horányi, A., Muñoz Sabater, J., Nicolas, J., Peubey, C., Radu, R., Rozum, I., Schepers, D., Simmons, A., Soci, C., Dee, D., Thépaut, J-N. (2023). ERA5 monthly averaged data on single levels from 1940 to present. Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Climate Data Store (CDS). https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.f17050d7

**Caveats**

A reanalysis is a model constrained by observations, not a measurement, and ERA5's assimilated observing system changed across 1940–present — so a trend in an ERA5 variable is not automatically a trend in the atmosphere. That matters less for the discontinuity it is first used to test, which is a step at one specific year unrelated to ERA5's own history, than it would for a claim about the whole record. Monthly means smooth away the daily extremes that drive rainfall screening, so this bounds whether the climate moved rather than measuring what any individual night looked like. 0.25° cells over a 32 km radar footprint means a station near a sharp precipitation gradient is represented worse than one inland. Access needs a personal access token AND a one-off acceptance of the `cc-by` licence.

## CMIP6 DAMIP and historical — near-surface air temperature, detection and attribution

- **id** `cmip6_damip`
- **drivers only**, no evidence rows · **realm** `aerial`
- **landing page** https://pcmdi.llnl.gov/CMIP6/
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
  - Most CMIP6 output is CC BY 4.0, but the licence is set per modelling centre and a few are non-commercial. Any published product built on a specific model must carry that model's own terms, which is why the citation names the centres rather than only the project.
- **sensitivity** `not_sensitive` by default

**Cite as**

> Eyring, V., Bony, S., Meehl, G. A., Senior, C. A., Stevens, B., Stouffer, R. J., Taylor, K. E. (2016). Overview of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) experimental design and organization. Geoscientific Model Development 9, 1937–1958. https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-1937-2016 — with Gillett, N. P. et al. (2016), Detection and Attribution Model Intercomparison Project (DAMIP v1.0), Geoscientific Model Development 9, 3685–3697, https://doi.org/10.5194/gmd-9-3685-2016, and the individual modelling centres credited per model as CMIP6 terms require.

**Caveats**

`hist-nat` is a counterfactual: it is what the models say the climate would have done under solar and volcanic forcing alone, and it must never be presented as an observation. Models are 1–2° so a station-point sample is regional rather than local. `historical` ends in 2014, so the window both experiments share stops there while the observed record runs to 2025 — the attribution therefore uses a *ratio* from the models and a magnitude from observations, which is what makes the mismatch tolerable. A run starting in 1995 also begins in the recovery from Pinatubo, which can give `hist-nat` a positive trend from volcanic rebound alone and understate the human share, so the window is varied and both answers reported. Member counts are wildly uneven (fifty for MIROC6 and CanESM5, three for nine others), so members are averaged within a model before models are averaged together.

## Southern African Bird Atlas Project (SABAP1) — atlas cards, 1987–1991

- **id** `sabap1`
- **evidence type** `survey_index` · **realm** `terrestrial` · **taxon scope** `exact`
- **landing page** https://www.gbif.org/dataset/282d0ccb-4fa0-40f9-8593-105c77e88417
- **licence** [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
- **redistribution** permitted, attribution required
- **sensitivity** `low` by default

**Cite as**

> South African National Biodiversity Institute. Southern African Bird Atlas Project. Version 1.0. Occurrence dataset https://doi.org/10.15468/ry4ux6 accessed via GBIF.org on 2026-07-30. Underlying atlas: Harrison, J. A., Allan, D. G., Underhill, L. G., Herremans, M., Tree, A. J., Parker, V., Brown, C. J. (eds) (1997). The Atlas of Southern African Birds. BirdLife South Africa, Johannesburg.

**Caveats**

Citizen science, so effort is not fixed by design the way a trawl survey's is: cards per cell over the 1987–1991 core run from 4 at the tenth percentile to 119 at the ninetieth and 2,271 at the maximum, which is why reporting rate is stored as cards-with-species over cards and why the consistent-footprint rule from Phase 1b has to be applied before any comparison. Presence only — `occurrenceStatus` is empty for all 5,053,399 rows — so an absence is the absence of a row and the denominator has to come from the cards. Dates are month resolution: the `day` column holds 1, 28, 30 or 31, the ends of a month rather than an observation date. Years in the archive run from 1901 to 2975, both impossible, so the ingest keeps 1950–1999 and logs what it drops. 830 of 98,878 cards carry records in two cells and are counted once per cell, because a card that touches two cells contributed effort to both. The cell id is derived from the cell centre rather than reusing the atlas's quarter-degree letter codes, so it stays checkable against the coordinates in the same row.
